extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, political scientists, public policy researchers, and students studying rulemaking and public participation
extracted.subtask_description: Theory-driven criteria and observable implications for identifying, classifying, and assessing public pressure (mass comment) campaigns in federal rulemaking, including motivations, indicators of organized activity, and expected patterns across public vs. private interest sponsors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a public pressure campaign / campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'campaign' is a batch of form-letter comments associated with an organization (as identified by the agency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by Potter and Balla et al. to operationalize mass comment campaigns; often identified where many comments share text or are linked to the same sponsoring organization. Example: Balla et al. code campaigns as form-letter batches associated with an organization and distinguish 'regulated' vs 'regulatory beneficiary' sponsors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of organized/cooperative comment activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments mediated through public pressure campaigns often (1) mention the name of the organization that mobilized them and (2) contain text similar or identical to other comments in the campaign, reflecting coordination through form/template letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observable markers that distinguish organized/mobilized comments from individual submissions; such features eliminate novel technical informational value. Also includes bulk mailing/upload patterns and the absence of original text. Empirical tests should look for repeated text strings, organization identifiers, or metadata showing bulk submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass comment campaigns as political information (petition/poll analog)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public pressure campaigns function like a petition or poll, capturing the intensity of preferences among the attentive public — i.e., how many people are willing to take the time to engage — and signaling political information to policymakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaign language often frames mobilization as public opinion (examples: World Wildlife Fund citing an opinion poll; Oceana calling its mobilization a petition signed by tens of thousands). Campaigns may thus be interpreted as measures of latent public demand or intensity, not as sources of technical expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usual Suspects vs Underdogs (Astroturf vs Conflict Expansion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two competing theoretical roles for campaigns: (a) 'Usual suspects' — well-resourced interests use campaigns to create an impression of public support (astroturf), legitimizing existing powerful actors; (b) 'Underdogs' — less-resourced groups use campaigns to expand the scope of conflict and reveal latent public support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative implications differ: if astroturf dominates, campaigns may be normatively suspect; if conflict expansion dominates, campaigns can counterbalance concentrated interests. Empirically test by assessing who sponsors campaigns and whether campaigns reinforce or counter existing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaign aims: expand scope of conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: One aim of public pressure campaigns is to expand the scope of the political conflict so that new audiences, media attention, or other actors become relevant to the policy fight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potter's theorized reasons include expanding conflict scope, growing/maintaining organizations, and giving agency leaders political cover. Empirical signals include co-occurrence with protests, congressional activity, or media coverage and campaigns launched proactively to broaden attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaign aims: organizational growth and political cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns may aim primarily to grow or maintain advocacy organizations (collect contact info, recruit members, fundraise) or to provide political cover for agency leaders to pursue policies despite opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for performative features (e.g., consent to periodic communication, 'thank you' campaigns), use of campaigns for contact-list building, and statements framing campaigns as credit claiming or as supporting agency decisionmakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of pressure-campaign motivations (taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns can be distinguished by motivation: proactive going public, reactive counter-mobilization, credit claiming (targeting non-policymaker audiences when expecting to win), and 'going down fighting' (performative mobilization when expecting to lose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each motivation predicts different observable patterns: proactive campaigns skew toward the mobilizing side, reactive campaigns are smaller and may use deception, credit-claiming emphasizes publicity/association, and going-down-fighting emphasizes member satisfaction/recruitment rather than policy impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proactive campaigns (going public)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coalitions 'go public' when they believe expanding the scope of conflict gives them an advantage; these campaigns often skew heavily toward the mobilizing side and may produce indirect increased effort (media, longer comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect higher volumes of genuine participation, potential media attention, and campaigns initiated even when the policy is only plausibly contestable. Mechanism: organizations reveal latent public support to persuade policymakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reactive campaigns (countermobilization)
rubrics_metrics.description: When one coalition goes public, opposing coalitions may launch reactive campaigns to emphasize that 'both sides' have public support; these campaigns typically engage fewer people and may sometimes use deceptive tactics (astroturf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reactive campaigns are expected to be smaller, possibly rely on paid or fabricated participation, and commonly appear only in response to an opposing campaign rather than unilaterally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit claiming and going-down-fighting (performative mobilization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns that primarily satisfy audiences other than policymakers: credit claiming to associate with positive policy developments when expecting to win, or going down fighting to energize and retain supporters when expecting to lose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These campaigns prioritize member engagement, fundraising, reputation-building, and long-term capacity over immediate policy change. Empirically look for collection of contact info, messaging aimed at supporters, and low investment in technical submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public pressure campaigns complement (not substitute) technical lobbying
rubrics_metrics.description: Public pressure campaigns are typically part of a broader lobbying coalition that also engages in sophisticated technical/legal lobbying; mass comments are a resource supporting inside strategies rather than replacing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis 2.2 predicts coalitions that mobilize will include actors submitting technical comments. Empirical approach: group organizations into coalitions and test whether campaigns co-occur with technical submissions from allied groups (e.g., Sierra Club Legal Team vs Digital Team example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observable implication: most public participation is organized (Hypothesis 2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals are more likely to participate as part of organized, cooperative activity rather than as independent 'citizen-initiated contacts'; barriers to individual participation make organized campaigns more common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testable by measuring the share of comments that show coordination markers (identical text, organization mention, bulk uploads) versus unique individual submissions. Behavioral mechanism: organizations reduce costs, inform and motivate participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsor pattern: public-interest groups sponsor campaigns more often (Hypothesis 2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public interest (advocacy) coalitions are more likely than private/business coalitions to sponsor mass comment campaigns because they have incentives both to influence policy via scope expansion and to mobilize members for organizational reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potter and others find advocacy campaigns generate more comments on average than industry campaigns. Empirical tests can compare frequency and size of campaigns by sponsor type and whether campaigns are initiated by advocacy groups in the absence of industry campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response magnitude: public-interest campaigns get larger responses (Hypothesis 2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a given mobilization effort, coalitions representing broad public interests should elicit larger public responses than private interest coalitions, because they draw on broader latent public support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize by comparing volume-per-outreach or response-per-solicitation between public-interest and private-interest campaigns; expect larger average campaign sizes for advocacy groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational capacity: campaigns run by large national policy advocacy organizations (Hypothesis 2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass mobilizations targeting national policy typically require significant organizing capacity and thus are most commonly run by large national policy advocacy organizations or coalitions of membership organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for sponsors with sufficient membership/resources; evidence includes identification of commenters as members, centralized campaign infrastructure, and organization-level metadata (e.g., Sierra Club's contact-collection practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private interest campaigns are typically reactive (Hypothesis 2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrow private interests (e.g., business-led coalitions) generally launch public pressure campaigns reactively in response to opposing campaigns rather than unopposed, because expanding the scope of conflict usually disadvantages them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test by measuring instances of unopposed campaigns by sponsor type; expect private-interest campaigns to co-occur with opposing advocacy campaigns and to be less common as unopposed mobilizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional receptivity moderates campaign effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies have different mechanisms for processing technical versus political information; differential receptivity affects whether and how political information from mass engagement influences policy outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate institutional features (agency norms, use of expertise, procedural rules) into models: even large campaigns may have limited effect where agencies prioritize technical/legal inputs. This moderates the causal pathway depicted in the coalition model.
